To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) larger rates of change in gradient can be achieved at threshold for peripheral nerve activation with the addition of a uniform field that varies synchronously with the gradient; and 2) the increase in rate of change is larger for transverse coils than for axial coils.
larger rates of gradient switching can be achieved with concomitant field compensation coils, but the benefits of these coils depend on the body position of the subject.
larger rates of gradient switching at the threshold for stimulation of peripheral nerves are possible when a uniform concomitantly varying field is applied synchronously with a gradient.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing methods for reducing peripheral nerve stimulation due gradient switching in MRI.
the use of additional concomitant fields in the design of gradient coils to reduce peripheral nerve stimulation.
the design and construction of gradient coil systems that are able to produce large rates of change of the magnetic field (gradient) with time without causing peripheral nerve stimulation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the addition of a uniform concomitants field coil to an actively shielded gradient coil system will increase the rate of change at the threshold for nerve stimulation, and this effect is larger for transverse than for axial coils, depending on body position.

a significant improvement in the maximum rate of change of field that can be achieved at a peripheral nerve stimulation threshold is possible by the addition of a concomitant field, but the magnitude of this improvement is dependent upon both the coil design and body location of the subject.

, for the particular design of coils used here and for the specific body positions investigated, the increase in the rate‐of‐change of gradient at threshold for peripheral nerve‐stimulation that could be achieved with the addition of the concomitant field was significantly greater in the transverse coils than in the axial coils.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we can reduce the rate at which the magnetic field changes in time (the rate of change of the gradient), which can reduce the peripheral nerve stimulation.

the addition of a concomitant field to a gradient coil can increase the rate at which the gradient can change at the threshold for nerve stimulation, without significantly reducing the spatial extent of a region over which imaging could be carried out.

we have demonstrated that it is possible to increase the gradient performance in terms of the rate of change with time of the gradient field at the threshold for stimulation without significant reduction in the spatial extent of region over which imaging could be performed by applying a concomitant field.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can reduce the peripheral nerve stimulation (PNS) by using a uniform concomitent field.
the use of additional uniform fields can be used to improve the performance of gradient coils.

the addition of a uniform field coil to an actively shielded gradient system can increase the maximum gradient slew rate that can be achieved at a fixed threshold for peripheral nerve activation without a significant reduction in the spatial extent of regions in which imaging can be performed.
